item.title: Oil Prices Jump on Energy Supply Worries
item.description:
Oil prices jumped and stock futures fell slightly on Sunday on concerns that energy supplies from the Persian Gulf would be further diminished by a drone attack on a critical pipeline in Saudi Arabia.

The Saudi Arabian Energy Ministry said it was closing the pipeline as a precautionary measure, but the shutdown came after reports that the Houthi militia had seized a strategic Red Sea island and a port city, which could further choke shipping in the area. Already, most shipping in the nearby Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, has been halted.

Adding to the uncertainty in the region, a planned meeting between Iran and several Gulf Arab countries it has attacked during the war was indefinitely postponed on Sunday.

The price of Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil, rose to about $108 a barrel, about 3.2 percent, when markets opened on Sunday.

West Texas Intermediate crude, the U.S. benchmark, was up a little under $103 a barrel, about 2.9 percent.

Investors and analysts are focused on the continued disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that is a vital trading route for oil and natural gas. Before the war as much as one-fifth of the world’s oil supply passed through it.

Futures on the S&P 500 pointed to a small decline, a little over half a percentage point, when stocks resume trading in the United States on Monday.

Gas prices held steady over the weekend, at a national average of $4.31 a gallon, according to the AAA motor club. But prices at the pump have risen by about 16 cents a gallon in the last week. Prices for a gallon of regular gas are now nearly 45 percent higher than they were before the war began.

Gas prices don’t move in lock step with crude, usually trailing increases or drops by a few days.

The average price of diesel continues to rise. It was $6.20 a gallon on Sunday, up about 65 percent since the start of the war.

item.title: The Bari Weiss Era of ‘60 Minutes’ Begins
item.description:
The Serious Newsperson cast of correspondents was different — goodbye, Scott Pelley; hello, Ross Douthat — and the production values seemed glossier, a little more Vice News than Huntley-Brinkley Report.

But for all the Sturm und Drang that has surrounded “60 Minutes” since the arrival of CBS News’s high-profile editor in chief, Bari Weiss, the version of America’s most watched news program that returned to CBS on Sunday looked a lot like the show viewers have come to expect.

Norah O’Donnell landed a gripping interview with an Air Force colonel who recounted his harrowing rescue from behind enemy lines after being shot down over Iran. Lesley Stahl presented an investigation into middlemen who charge large sums to lobby for presidential pardons. A lighter segment profiled Sean McVay, the coach of the Los Angeles Rams.

There were some changes. The pardon segment revived the use of a hidden camera, a once-common technique at “60 Minutes” that had dwindled in recent years. The show’s signature ticking stopwatch received a makeover, and the “book” graphics that used to appear behind correspondents were replaced with sleek screens.

And for those wondering how the new season would treat President Trump, the program referred to the war in Iran as “costly and unpopular,” and said he had pardoned “a string of unrepentant financial con men,” as well as “rioters” at the United States Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021.

The formula of politics, sports and accountability journalism was the same mix that has frequently kept “60 Minutes,” 59 seasons in, among the 10 most watched network shows of the week.

Off-camera, however, the season premiere came after a period of wrenching change at the program that threatened its reputation.

Ms. Weiss purged the program’s senior leadership this year, and many star correspondents, including Mr. Pelley and Anderson Cooper, either quit or were forced out; Mr. Pelley accused her of “murdering” the program, an incident that led to his dismissal. Some of those who exited said Ms. Weiss tried to inject political bias, a claim that CBS News has denied.

As a result, Ms. Weiss and her pick to oversee “60 Minutes,” the technology journalist and filmmaker Nick Bilton, zeroed in on the season premiere as a critical test to placate skeptical viewers — and media executives who wondered why Ms. Weiss had insisted on overhauling CBS News’s most successful franchise.

Besides securing the interviews necessary for a newsy episode, CBS also created a slick ad campaign with a new slogan — “It’s Time” — and hired a celebrity photographer, Mark Seliger, to shoot a glossy photograph of the cast in Grand Central Terminal. (One version of the photo includes Mr. Bilton in a slick suit; in another version, he is not there.)

The premiere seemed calibrated to anticipate criticism that the revamped “60 Minutes” would go too hard, or too soft, on Mr. Trump.

CBS’s parent company, Paramount, paid $16 million to settle a lawsuit that Mr. Trump filed in 2024 over “60 Minutes”; soon after, the Trump administration approved Paramount’s sale to the tech scion David Ellison. Mr. Ellison, who appointed Ms. Weiss, has maintained ties with Mr. Trump, hosting him and his senior aides for a dinner in Washington in April. The result has been intense scrutiny on CBS News’s political coverage.

On Sunday, the airman segment featured an interview with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who rarely speaks one on one with major news outlets outside his former employer, Fox News; Mr. Hegseth used an expletive in his interview that CBS bleeped out.

The program’s quest to land an interview with the downed colonel, known as Dude 44 Bravo, involved executives from the new and old editions of “60 Minutes.”

Keith Sharman, the segment’s producer, began reaching out to sources to secure the interview on April 6, within hours of the rescue, according to a person connected to the show. He and Tanya Simon, the “60 Minutes” executive producer who was fired in May, attended a meeting arranged by Ms. Weiss with Tami Radabaugh, an adviser to Mr. Hegseth, to make their case, two people connected to the show said. The interview was ultimately booked this summer.

Ms. Stahl’s segment on pardons was the result of a monthslong effort by “60 Minutes” and the investigative team at CBS News — a collaboration within the news division that has been comparatively rare in the past but is now actively encouraged by Mr. Bilton and Ms. Weiss.

Ms. Stahl concluded with a statement from the Trump administration, which said any suggestion the president had behaved unethically “is either ill-informed or malicious.”

Sunday’s episode made no mention of the behind-the-scenes drama at the program. Instead, Mr. Douthat, a former columnist at The New York Times, offered a closing message about artificial intelligence fears. He said that for six decades “60 Minutes” had “meant the same thing: journalism you can trust. Where we’re headed, we’re going to need it.”

One important verdict on the season premiere will have to wait. Last season, “60 Minutes” averaged 9.1 million Americans an episode, up 9 percent from the year before. Nielsen is expected to report Sunday’s ratings on Tuesday.
